summary: Deep dive into async KV prefetch strategies and kernel-mapper heuristics comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths. Discussed memory-bound vs compute-bound kernels, CUDA graph replay instability at high seq lengths, NUMA effects on host-device transfers, and on-prem VPC networking considerations. Agreed to exchange microbenchmarks and run a pilot on Helix's NVLink cluster.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-04-12
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Recording: yes

[00:00] Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. Quick intros?
[00:12] Samir (Helix): Samir here, I run ML infra. Leah's on the line for SRE stuff, Tom our CTO will listen in later.
[00:20] Jamie: Great. Ravi, wanna kick off high-level agenda?
[00:23] Ravi (Redwood SE): Sure—today we wanted to look at async KV prefetch patterns, how kernel mapper picks TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels vs vllm paths, and where cudagraph replay can cause hiccups at long sequences or mixed-quant workloads. We'll also touch on on-prem networking implications since you mentioned NVLink cluster.
[00:40] Leah (Helix): Yes, we run 4x A100 NVLink per node and a mix of PCIe-only boxes. Primary ask is predictable p95 and cost savings with quantization but not breaking tail latency.
[00:52] Ravi: Perfect. Quick context: we benchmarked two paradigms—one where KV prefetch is synchronous at token emission and one where we prefetch asynchronously across streams while the previous token is executing. The tradeoffs are memory pressure and increased concurrency.
[01:15] Samir: We're most worried about memory-bound hits when we prefetch across many concurrent sessions, we saw OOM in some initial tests.
[01:22] Ravi: Right. In our internal tests on TRT-LLM (TensorRT-LLM) the kernel-mapper will choose fused attention kernels for contiguous, low-seq workloads; but once KV gets large or fragmented the mapper falls back to more generic kernels which have different memory footprints. With vLLM, its lazy KV management tends to keep smaller persistent caches but more host-device chatter in some cases.
[01:50] Tom (Helix): Can you clarify "mapper falls back"—is that dynamic at runtime or compile-time?
[01:56] Ravi: Mostly runtime. There's a decision layer that evaluates expected sequence length distribution and memory availability. If the allocator predicts eviction thrash, it selects kernels that avoid large intermediate buffers. That prediction can be wrong if your input distribution changes unexpectedly—hence nondeterminism during cudagraph replay sometimes.
[02:20] Jamie: We have an example trace we can share—shows a cudagraph replay failing at seq=2048 after a quantized path switch.
[02:29] Leah: We saw similar in our stress tests—CUDA graph replay would crash on long sequences but only when memory fragmentation was high. It took a reboot to clear.
[02:37] Ravi: That's a sign of fragmentation + pinned memory exhaustion. Two mitigations: 1) async prefetch with bounded in-flight keys (so we limit KV pages concurrently resident), 2) ensure cudagraph capture includes worst-case memory layout or avoid capture for those specific paths. Both have tradeoffs—capture avoids costly kernel launch overhead, non-capture is slower but more stable.
[03:05] Samir: For async prefetch, how do you bound in-flight? Token window?
[03:09] Ravi: Usually a combination—prefetch horizon (e.g., lookahead of 6 tokens) + per-model resident pages cap. We also employ eviction-aware batching so batches that would push resident pages above threshold get routed to a lower-cost model or queued.
[03:27] Jamie: Quick interjection—Helix, do you have strict tail SLAs for p99 or are you p95 focused?
[03:33] Tom: p99 is critical for user-facing latency < 400ms. p95 can be higher but we want stable p99.
[03:40] Ravi: Ok so candidly, candiate approach: TRT-LLM with aggressive fused kernels + persistent KV is best for throughput and lower cost per token but requires careful memory shaping and sometimes disables cudagraph capture on non-deterministic branches. vLLM's path gives more graceful memory scaling but you might pay slightly more per token due to extra transfers and kernel launches.
[04:04] Leah: What about mixed quantization? We plan to use 4-bit matrix weights and keep activations in 8-bit for certain heads to preserve quality.
[04:13] Ravi: Mixed quant is fine but it can cause kernel-path jitter. Some fused kernels assume 8-bit activations; they will fall back if types mismatch which changes memory and execution time. We recommend a quantization profile per model and a small warmup to prime the kernel mapper. Also the mapper can be forced via env flags if you need deterministic pathing for p99.
[04:38] Samir: Can you walk us through an example nvprof/nvtx trace where the failure happened?
[04:43] Ravi: Yep, we uploaded a trace (link shared in chat). In the trace you can see at ~00:25 the cudagraph replay tries to replay a sequence of launches; one kernel returns CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED after memory alloc in the middle of the graph. There's small device-side allocation from a fallback kernel not present in the fused path. It's subtle and shows up only at high seq because only then the fallback path is used.
[05:12] Jamie: Note: our microbenchmark includes a togglable "force fallback" flag so you can reproduce the slower path deterministically.
[05:18] Tom: For on-prem, RDMA between hosts concerns us—does Redwood use host staging for KV or direct GPU-GPU via NVLink?
[05:25] Ravi: We prefer NVLink resident KV when available; host staging is only used for cross-node or PCIe-only machines. For cross-node we use RDMA-assisted DMA but performance depends on NIC type. On Mellanox HDR with GPUDirect RDMA we get good host-less transfers; on standard 10/25GbE you will see heavier host CPU involvement and jitter.
[05:48] Leah: We have Mellanox HDR so NVLink + GPUDirect is possible. Are there specific kernel/allocator flags to enable GPUDirect path?
[05:56] Ravi: Yes, it's an infra-level switch. We'll provide the config. Two caveats: RDMA adds complexity to memory registration and can exacerbate fragmentation if not coordinated with the allocator. Also kernel mapper sometimes biases to device-local buffers for fused kernels; that helps keep latency lower.
[06:18] Samir: How do you benchmark fairly? Our ops team kept getting different p95 numbers depending on prompt distribution.
[06:24] Jamie: Good point—benchmark methodology we recommend: 1) run representative prompt length distribution (share your 95th percentile), 2) 3 phases: cold start, warmup (5k tokens), steady-state (30k tokens), 3) measure p50/p95/p99 and tailcoalescence across DACs, 4) include model switch scenarios where mapper might swap kernels mid-run.
[06:50] Ravi: Also capture nvtx ranges for KV prefetch, host->device, and kernel exec. That shows where the latency spikes are—if it's memcpy H2D or kernel kernel.
[07:02] Samir: We saw spikes in memcpy H2D during peak concurrency. Is that because of stream saturation?
[07:08] Ravi: Could be. Streams and priorities matter—async prefetch should use low-priority streams for prefetch copies, occlude them with higher priority compute streams to avoid head-of-line blocking. But if your NIC saturates, copies will still contend.
[07:24] Leah: Any tips for NUMA? We've got multi-socket boxes feeding a single GPU set.
[07:30] Ravi: Pinning is essential. On multi-socket hosts, ensure the CPU affinity for the io threads that orchestrate H2D transfers is on the same NUMA node as the GPU. Otherwise, you'll pay remote memory latency for all staged pages. We include numa-bind scripts in the repo we share.
[07:49] Tom: Ok, let's talk about fallback routing—if the mapper decides a model will exceed memory, can Redwood route to a slower model variant rather than fail?
[07:57] Jamie: Yes, that's part of our smart routing. For Dedicated customers we can provision a compatible lower-memory quantized variant automatically and route overflow traffic there. That increases cost a bit but preserves p99 SLAs.
[08:12] Samir: How much extra cost are we likely to see on fallback? ballpark?
[08:15] Ravi: Depends on weight. If you route to 4-bit vs 8-bit, token op cost drops. Routing to a smaller capacity but same model often increases latency by 10–40% depending on batch. We have cost models and an example spreadsheet we'll share.
[08:30] Leah: About cudagraph capture—you suggested capturing the worst-case layout. How do you force that in practice?
[08:36] Ravi: Trick is to run a synthetic capture pass that allocates KV at maximum expected size and then capture. It increases initial memory but makes replay stable. Alternatively, disable capture on paths that mutate allocator behavior heavily.
[08:49] Tom: Do you have any production examples where async prefetch saved tail latency?
[08:53] Ravi: Yes—a customer in ads saw p95 drop 30% with async prefetch + bounded horizon, because compute overlapped with memcpy rather than serializing. But they had to tune resident caps to avoid fragmentation. We'll anonymize that trace.
[09:08] Jamie: Let's surface the specific artifacts we'll share: microbenchmark repo, env flags to force mapper behavior, numa-bind scripts, and an example cudagraph capture repro. Links will be posted to the calendar invite.
[09:18] Samir: Great. A few quick clarifying q's from Leah: 1) if we disable capture for some flows, does Redwood's runtime pay more? 2) If gpudirect is enabled, does that reduce fragmentation risk?
[09:28] Ravi: 1) Yes—no capture has higher per-token overhead due to kernel launch costs, but it's more stable. 2) gpudirect reduces CPU involvement but fragmentation risk remains; in fact, GPUDirect can make fragmentation symptoms appear earlier because pages are registered huge and persist. That's why allocator policy changes are recommended alongside gpudirect.
[09:50] Leah: Understood.
[09:53] Jamie: Ok we'll pause and let folks breathe. Any more deep technical Qs or should we move to next steps?
[10:00] Tom: One more—how does Redwood handle model upgrades mid-flight? If we rollout a quantized update, will the mapper gracefully switch?
[10:07] Ravi: We do staged rollouts and can pin existing sessions to old versions for a while. For mid-flight policy we can do model-version pinning per token and drain active sessions before switching unless you opt-in for immediate cutover. That avoids mapper oscillation.
[10:23] Samir: Good, that's important.
[10:25] Jamie: Okay recap and next steps: Ravi will share microbenchmarks + trace and a docker image. Ana will draft pilot doc. Helix runs script on NVLink nodes and shares logs. We'll reconvene week of 2027-04-19.
[10:38] Leah: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:41] Tom: Thanks.
[10:45] Jamie: End meeting—recording saved.
